<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This repository is a “terraform-infra-common” library: a curated collection of reusable Terraform modules that encapsulate common Google Cloud Run and event-driven patterns, plus accompanying Go-based helper programs (under cmd/ and modules/*/cmd/) and shared libraries (pkg/).  
   - Its main goal is to provide building blocks for infra-as-code: Cloud Run services (trampolines, brokers, recorders), Pub/Sub triggers, BigQuery sinks, Cloud SQL, dashboards, GitHub bots, networking, etc.

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top level  
     • cmd/replayer – a Go CLI  
     • pkg/ – shared Go libraries (http metrics, pubsub, workqueue, profilers, etc.)  
     • modules/ – ~30 self-contained Terraform modules. Some modules include Go code under modules/*/cmd/ which is built into container images and deployed by the Terraform module.  
     • .github/workflows – CI pipelines for Go tests, Terraform validation, docs generation.  
     • hack/update-docs.sh, README.md, go.mod – build and documentation orchestration.

3. Examine the README  
   - Confirms: “A repository containing a collection of common infrastructure modules for encapsulating common Cloud Run patterns.”  
   - Usage: top-level Terraform provides a google provider, then consumers import these modules from Terraform Registry.

4. How to draw an accurate system design diagram  
   a. Main components  
      • Developer & CI/CD (GitHub Actions)  
      • Terraform Registry / Module consumers  
      • Terraform CLI (Cloud or local)  
      • Container Build & Registry (e.g., GCR/Artifact Registry)  
      • Google Cloud infra:  
         – Cloud Run services (from modules/*/cmd)  
         – Pub/Sub topics & subscriptions  
         – Cloud Storage buckets  
         – BigQuery datasets/tables  
         – Cloud SQL instances  
         – GKE clusters & Load Balancers  
         – IAM (Service Accounts, GitHub Workload Identity Federation)  
         – Cloud Monitoring dashboards & alerting  
      • External integrations: GitHub API (for bots), third-party events.

   b. Relationships & interactions  
      1. Developer push → GitHub Actions pipelines run:  
         – go tests (pkg/, modules/*/cmd/)  
         – terraform fmt/lint/validate (modules/)  
         – hack/update-docs → regenerate module docs  
         – build & push Docker images for Go commands  
         – publish modules to Terraform Registry  
      2. Consumer’s Terraform CLI  
         – fetches modules from Registry  
         – provisions GCP resources: creates container images, deploys Cloud Run services, sets up Pub/Sub topics/triggers, configures BigQuery, SQL, dashboards, networking, IAM.  
      3. Event-driven flows  
         – Cloud Storage or GitHub events trigger Cloud Run trampolines → Pub/Sub → CloudEvents broker → recorders or pull triggers → downstream systems (BigQuery, Cloud SQL, dashboards).  
      4. Monitoring & Alerting  
         – Modules/dashboard and modules/alerting create Cloud Monitoring dashboards and alerting policies based on deployed services and metrics emitted via pkg/httpmetrics.

   c. Architectural patterns & design principles  
      - Modular IaC: each Terraform module encapsulates one concern (service, event, database, networking).  
      - Microservices on Cloud Run: packaged Go binaries (trampolines, recorders, brokers).  
      - Event-driven architecture via Pub/Sub and CloudEvents.  
      - Separation of concerns: shared code in pkg/, one CLI per module when needed.  
      - CI/CD-as-code: GitHub workflows enforce code quality and maintain module registry.

   d. Key technologies & frameworks  
      - Terraform + HCL modules  
      - Go: cmd/ and modules/*/cmd and pkg/ libraries  
      - Google Cloud Platform: Cloud Run, Pub/Sub, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, GKE, IAM, Monitoring  
      - Docker/Container Registry  
      - GitHub Actions, Dependabot, style checks

5. Tailoring the diagram for this project type  
   - Emphasize the module-centric view: each box under “Terraform modules” contains its own sub-components (e.g., “cloudevent-broker module” builds ingress binary → Cloud Run → Pub/Sub topic).  
   - Show two tiers:  
     1. Build/Publish tier (GitHub → CI pipelines → module registry + container images)  
     2. Deployment tier (Consumer Terraform → GCP infra + event flows).  
   - Highlight event flows between modules (Pub/Sub → Cloud Run services → BigQuery).

6. Diagramming guidelines  
   – Use clear, descriptive labels: “GitHub Actions”, “Terraform Registry”, “Consumer Terraform CLI”, “Cloud Run: bucket-events-trampoline”, “Pub/Sub: bucket-events-topic”, etc.  
   – Draw directional arrows for data/control flow: e.g., Developer → GitHub Actions → Module Publish; Terraform CLI → Cloud Run Deploy; Bucket → Pub/Sub → Recorder → BigQuery.  
   – Color-code component types:  
     • CI/CD (blue),  
     • Terraform modules (green),  
     • GCP infra (yellow),  
     • Go containers (orange),  
     • External services (gray).  
   – Use distinct shapes for boundaries:  
     • Rectangle for modules,  
     • Cylinder for databases,  
     • Cloud icon for GCP services,  
     • Document icon for Terraform Registry.

7. Detail & completeness  
   - Represent each Terraform module as an individual box or group by category (eventing, storage, compute, monitoring).  
   - Expand on modules that include Go binaries: draw the build step → Docker image → Cloud Run service.  
   - Capture all major resource types (Pub/Sub, BigQuery, Cloud SQL, GKE, etc.) and show how modules orchestrate them.  
   - Avoid over-aggregating: better to show many small boxes than to hide details.  
   - The final diagram should reveal the end-to-end flow from code commit to deployed event-driven infra, illustrating how the reusable modules and Go programs interconnect.
</explanation>
